### Question 1


The data below refers to violent crime rates for a random sample of 20 American areas in 2013 and
2015. The same areas are used both years so the samples are paired. The values show the number
of reported crimes per 100,000 population.

```{r}
y2013=c(613.8, 453.1, 826.7, 322.2, 640.9, 807.1, 716.7, 190.9, 217.7, 
125.1, 553.1, 914.1, 409.6, 53.7, 487.8, 342.8, 120, 171.8, 190.9, 
237.2)
y2015=c(610.5, 571.2, 1157.2, 485.5, 934.6, 950.1, 720.1, 288, 298.6, 
75.7, 575.8, 1072.1, 631, 33.3, 460.2, 377, 144.5, 161.5, 225.7, 
269.5)
```

We can construct a confidence interval using the command t.test, using the subcommmands conf.level=0.99 to control the confidence level and paired=T to specify that the data is paired.
```{r}
t.test(y2013,y2015,conf.level=0.99,paired=T)
```
The 99% CI for the difference in
population means, taking y2013-y2015, is 
$(-13.64, -151.1).$
Since 0 is not included
in the interval, it is likely that there is a difference between the years. It looks as if crime
has increased. This test is valid if the differences appear normally distributed. The stem
diagram and boxplot below are slightly skewed but do not show any major problems with normality.
```{r}
ydiff=y2013-y2015
stem(ydiff)
boxplot(ydiff)
```
```{r}
plot(y2013,y2015)
```
From the scatter plot we see that there is a strong positive correlation between y2013 and y2015. This means that it would not be valid to use the assumption that the random samples are independent. If we implement the non-paired test we get the following results:
```{r}
t.test(y2013,y2015,conf.level=0.99, paired=FALSE)
```

### Question 2

We have the following data
```{r}
data2=c(12.4, 16.7, 20.5, 17, 10.6, 14.9, 16.8, 21.6, 17.7, 10.2, 15.1, 
18.2, 19.3, 21, 15.8)
```

To obtain a $95\%$ confidence interval for the underlying population mean we use the pivotal quantity
$$
\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}}
$$
which is distributed according to a $t_{n-1}$-distribution assuming the underlying population is normally distributed. Let us investigate these assumptions with a box plot and histogram
```{r}
boxplot(data2, horizontal=T)
hist(data2)
```

We see no reason to reject the idea that the populations are normally distributed from the plots. Now we can perform the test
```{r}
t.test(data2, conf.level = 0.95)
```
We obtain the Confidence interval
$$
(14.58,18.45).
$$

Now if we perform a hypothesis test with
$$
H_0: \mu =18.5 \text{ vs } \mu\neq 18.5
$$
we have
```{r}
t.test(data2, alternative = "two.sided", mu = 18.5)
```

Since $18.5$ is not included in this CI it seems we can reject $H_0$ at a $95\%$ significance level. Moreover the $p$-value of 0.04566 there is some evidence to reject $H_0$. It seems that the data do not come from a population with mean 18.5.

### Question 3

For the hypothesis
$$
H_0: \mu=15 \text{ vs } H_1: \mu>15
$$
we use
```{r}
t.test(data2,alternative = "greater",mu=15)
```
Since the p-value is just over 0.05, there is weak evidence that the population mean is greater
than 15.

For the hypothesis
$$
H_0: \mu=14 \text{ vs } H_1: \mu>14
$$

we use
```{r}
t.test(data2,alternative = "greater",mu=14)
```
Since the $p$-value is very low, there is strong evidence that the population mean is greater than $14$.

For the hypothesis
$$
H_0: \mu=13 \text{ vs } H_1: \mu>13
$$

we use
```{r}
t.test(data2,alternative = "greater",mu=13)
```
The $p$-value here is $0.0008018$ so overwhelming evidence against the null hypothesis that the population mean is $13$.


### Question 4

```{r}
data4=c(241, 251, 258, 246, 202, 246, 246, 301, 260, 228, 275, 266, 
264, 250, 258, 265, 240, 227, 271, 306, 269, 252, 242, 274, 222, 
244, 218, 228, 247, 202, 287, 279, 242, 262, 268, 226, 303, 214, 
242, 233)
```

We perform a two-sided hypothesis test to test the hypothesis

$$
H_0: \mu=260 \text{ vs } H_1: \mu\neq 260
$$

```{r}
t.test(data4,alternative = "two.sided",mu=260,conf.level = 0.05)
```

The $p$-value suggests we have evidence to reject the null hypothesis. It does not seem
plausible that these data come from a population with mean $260$.

### Question 5

```{r}
pixel=c(68, 75, 65, 69, 70, 72, 65, 66, 58, 62)
negative=c(59, 61, 62, 57, 64, 57, 60, 61, 51, 55)
t.test(pixel, negative, var.equal = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
```

Since the $p$-value is $0.0002572$, there is overwhelming evidence that more facts are
remembered by the population of subjects who view the witness by ``pixilation'' than by
those who view the witness by ``negative image''.

### Question 6

```{r}
realdat=c(40, 35, 50, 55, 65, 55, 50, 35, 30, 50, 60, 40)
picture=c(30, 35, 45, 40, 50, 35, 55, 25, 30, 45, 40, 50)
t.test(realdat,picture,alternative="greater",paired=T)
```
The $p$-value of $0.01363$ means that we have evidence against the null hypothesis.
Therefore we can conclude that in the population, real spiders evoke greater levels of
anxiety as compared to pictures of spiders.
